question_text: Explain how Corpuscular theory predicts the speed of light in a medium, say water, to be greater than the speed of light in vacuum. Is the prediction confirmed by experimental determination of the speed of light in water? If not, which alternative picture of light is consistent with experiment?
answer_text: The speed of light in a medium is predicted to be greater than in vacuum due to the interaction of light particles with the medium. However, experimental results show that light travels slower in water than in vacuum, confirming the wave theory of light instead.
final_answer: Thus, the wave theory of light is consistent with experimental observations.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of both corpuscular and wave theories of light.

question_text: Use Huygens’ principle to deduce directly that a point object placed in front of a plane mirror produces a virtual image whose distance from the mirror is equal to the object distance from the mirror.
answer_text: According to Huygens' principle, every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets. When a point object is placed in front of a plane mirror, the wavefronts from the object reach the mirror and reflect back. The virtual image formed is at the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.
final_answer: Thus, the distance of the virtual image from the mirror is equal to the object distance from the mirror.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of Huygens' principle and basic reflection concepts.

question_text: In a single slit diffraction experiment, the width of the slit is made double the original width. How does this affect the size and intensity of the central diffraction band? In what way is diffraction from each slit related to the interference pattern in a double-slit experiment? When a tiny circular obstacle is placed in the path of light from a distant source, a bright spot is seen at the centre of the shadow of the obstacle. Explain why? Two students are separated by a 7 m partition wall in a room 10 m high. If both light and sound waves can bend around obstacles, how is it that the students are unable to see each other even though they can converse easily? Ray optics is based on the assumption that light travels in a straight line. Diffraction effects (observed when light propagates through small apertures/slits or around small obstacles) disprove this assumption. Yet the ray optics assumption is so commonly used in understanding location and several other properties of images in optical instruments. What is the justification?

parts.part_text: If the width of the slit is made double the original width, then the size of the central diffraction band reduces to half and the intensity of the central diffraction band increases up to four times.
parts.answer_text: The size of the central diffraction band reduces to half and the intensity increases up to four times.
parts.final_answer: Thus, the size of the central diffraction band is halved and its intensity is quadrupled.

parts.part_text: The interference pattern in a double-slit experiment is modulated by diffraction from each slit. The pattern is the result of the interference of the diffracted wave from each slit.
parts.answer_text: Diffraction from each slit modulates the interference pattern.
parts.final_answer: The interference pattern is influenced by the diffraction from each slit.

parts.part_text: When a tiny circular obstacle is placed in the path of light from a distant source, a bright spot is seen at the centre of the shadow of the obstacle. This is because light waves are diffracted from the edge of the circular obstacle, which interferes constructively at the centre of the shadow.
parts.answer_text: Light waves diffracted from the edge of the obstacle interfere constructively at the center.
parts.final_answer: This constructive interference produces a bright spot at the center of the shadow.

parts.part_text: The bending of waves by obstacles by a large angle is possible when the size of the obstacle is comparable to the wavelength of the waves. The wavelength of the light waves is too small in comparison to the size of the obstacle. Thus, the diffraction angle will be very small. Hence, the students are unable to see each other.
parts.answer_text: Students cannot see each other due to the small diffraction angle of light.
parts.final_answer: Thus, they are unable to see each other.

parts.part_text: The justification is that in ordinary optical instruments, the size of the aperture involved is much larger than the wavelength of the light used.
parts.answer_text: In optical instruments, the aperture size is larger than the wavelength of light.
parts.final_answer: This justifies the use of ray optics despite diffraction effects.

difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of diffraction and interference concepts.

question_text: Justify that the intensity is zero at angles of nλ/a in the single slit diffraction pattern.
answer_text: Consider that a single slit of width d is divided into n smaller slits. Each of these infinitesimally small slits sends zero intensity in direction θ. Hence, the combination of these slits will give zero intensity.
final_answer: Therefore, the intensity is zero at angles of nλ/a due to the cancellation of contributions from the individual slits.
